title: About us
content:
About us Domains Protocols Numbers About About IANA For the Internet to work as a single seamless network, technical
		identifiers must mean the same thing everywhere: network identifiers
        like domain names and IP addresses must be assigned to a single party
        and have the same meaning globally, and communication protocols
        must use codes that have the same interpretation by every software implementation.
		The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) maintains the authoritative
        public registries that record these allocations and definitions,
        providing a common global point of reference. Although the Internet is decentralized by design, a limited set of its
        technical elements require this globally coordinated administration.
        The IANA role is a public service. The registries we maintain are
        openly published, our services are provided without charge, and we act
        as a neutral steward implementing policies developed by the communities
        we serve. Much of our work involves processing requests for identifiers
        arising from technical standardization processes or submitted directly
        by users of IANA services. We assess each request carefully against
        the established policies governing the identifier’s allocation and use. Our responsibilities extend beyond maintaining the registries themselves. We
        also operate the systems used to publish the registries and their
        associated data, together with supporting operational services. These include
        infrastructure and events involved in producing, securing, and distributing
        key aspects of the DNS. The need for the IANA functions dates to the record-keeping activities that
        accompanied the earliest experiments leading to today’s Internet, and their
        origins can be traced to the 1970s. Today, the functions are performed by Public Technical Identifiers , a
        purpose-built affiliate of ICANN dedicated
        exclusively to delivering the IANA services. Explore News Announcements, publications and consultations from across the IANA
					functions. Performance How we are performing against our service level commitments, at a
					glance and in monthly reports. The Organization How the IANA functions are governed, overseen, planned, and
					continuously improved. Archive Historical documents from prior projects and services, and the master
					index of published reports. Contact us How to reach us with questions, requests, and feedback. title: Domain Name Services
content:
Domain Name Services Domains Protocols Numbers About Domain Name Services We operate and maintain a number of key aspects of the DNS, including the root zone, and
	    the .int and .arpa domains. The DNS Root Zone The root is the upper-most part of the DNS hierarchy, and involves delegating administrative
	                responsibility of “top-level domains”, which are the last segment of a domain name. .INT The .int top-level domain, designed for the sole use of
	                cross-national organisations, such as treaty organisations, that do not naturally fit into a
	                specific country’s top-level domain. .ARPA The .arpa domain is used internally by Internet protocols for
                    purposes not designed to be directly accessed, as defined in various technical standards. IDN Practices Repository A repository of permissible characters for different languages and writing systems provided for
                    registration by different domain registries, helping to foster internationalization. Label Generation Rulesets The rules governing which characters may be used in internationalised domain names, and which
                    labels are treated as variants of one another, for the root zone and as references for
                    second-level registries. Root Key Signing Key (DNSSEC) The Root Key Signing Key provides verification of the DNSSEC-signed root zone, administered
                through public key signing ceremonies and serving as the DNS trust anchor. Reserved Domains Specially designated domains that are held to serve specialized purposes, such
                    as avoiding conflicts with potential real-world usage. title: Root Zone Management
content:
Root Zone Management Domains Protocols Numbers About Root Zone Management The Domain Name System (DNS) root zone is the highest-level of the naming hierarchy, principally composed of
        delegations of top-level domains (such as .edu or .in ).
        In managing the DNS root zone, IANA responsibilities include assigning managers for these domains, recording
        technical delegation data in the root zone, and publishing a registry of related information. Top-level Domains The Top-Level Domain Registry (also known as the Root Zone Database ) is the authoritative
                    record of top-level domains, including the organization that manages the domains, technical
                    details and contact information. Files and Downloads The root zone DNS data is available for download as a DNS zone file along with associated trust
                    information, and in other formats. Delegation Management Existing TLD managers can maintain their delegation details through our online interface. Instructions and Guides Articles covering the rules governing what top-level domains are permissible, the procedures
                    to register and update top-level domains, and other related topics. Root Zone DNSSEC Information Information about DNSSEC in the root zone, including the trust anchor for the DNS.
